Jesus said to him, “If I spoke wrongly, testify about what I did wrong. But if I spoke rightly, why are you hitting me?”
Then Annas sent him, still bound, to Caiaphas the high priest.
Simon Peter was standing there, warming himself. They said to him, “You are not also one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it, saying, “No.”
One of the high priest’s servants, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said to him, “Wasn’t I the one who saw you with him in the garden?”
Peter denied it again, and immediately a rooster crowed.

After this, they took Jesus from Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not go inside the governor’s headquarters with him, so that they would not become defiled but could eat the Passover meal.
Pilate came out to them and said, “What accusation are you bringing against this man?”
They answered him, “If this man had not done wrong, we would not have handed him over to you.”
Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” The Jews said to him, “We are not permitted to put anyone to death.”
This was so that the words Jesus had spoken would be fulfilled, indicating what kind of death he was going to die.
Pilate went back inside the governor’s headquarters, called Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the king of the Jews?”
Jesus answered, “Are you saying this on your own, or did others tell you about me?”
Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests are the ones who handed you over to me. What have you done?”

Jesus answered, “My kingdom does not come from this world. If my kingdom came from this world, my servants would fight to keep me from being handed over to the Jews. But as it is, my kingdom does not come from here.”

Pilate then said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You are the one saying that I am a king. I was born for this, and I came into the world for this: to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.”
Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After saying this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them, “I find no grounds for an accusation against him.”
“But you have a custom that I release someone for you at Passover. Do you want me, then, to release the king of the Jews for you?”
They all shouted, “Do not release this man! Release Barabbas instead!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
Then Pilate took Jesus and had him whipped.
The soldiers wove a crown out of thorns, put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple robe.
They kept coming up to him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and slapping him.
Pilate came out to them again and said, “Look, I have brought him out to you so that you may know that I find no grounds for an accusation against him.”
Jesus came out with the crown of thorns on his head and the purple robe on him. He said to them, “Here is the man!”

When the chief priests and the attendants saw him, they shouted, “Crucify him! Crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no grounds for a charge against him.”
The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and according to our law he must die, because he made himself the Son of God.”
When Pilate heard these words, he became even more afraid.
He went back inside the governor’s headquarters and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus did not answer him.
Pilate then said to him, “Will you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have the authority to crucify you and the authority to release you?”
Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given to you from heaven. For this reason, the one who handed me over to you is guilty of a great sin.”
For this reason, Pilate was seeking to release him. But the Jews kept shouting, “If you release this man, you are no friend of the emperor. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes the emperor.”
When Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called Lithostrotos, or Gabbatha in Hebrew.
It was six o’clock on the day of Preparation for the Passover. He said to the Jews, “Here is your king!”
But they shouted, “Take him away! Take him away! Crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your king?” The chief priests answered, “We have no other king except Caesar.”
Then he handed him over to them to be crucified. They took Jesus and led him out.
He was carrying his cross, and he went out to a place called the Skull, or Golgotha in Hebrew.
There they crucified him, and two others with him, one on either side, with Jesus between them.
Pilate also wrote an inscription and fastened it to the cross. It read, “This is Jesus the Nazarene, the King of the Jews.”
Many of the Jews read this inscription because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. It was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek.
So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but, ‘He is the one who said, “I am the King of the Jews.”’”
Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

When the soldiers had crucified him, they took his clothing and divided it into four parts, one part for each soldier, and also took the tunic. The tunic had no seam, but was woven in a fourfold weave.

They said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it will be.” This was so that the scripture would be fulfilled: “They divided my clothes among themselves and cast lots for my garment.” The soldiers did these things.
Standing beside Jesus’ cross were his mother, his mother’s sister, Mary the daughter of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, here is your son.”
Then he said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” From that day on, the disciple took her into his home.
After these things, Jesus knew that everything was now completed. So that the scripture would be fulfilled, he said, “I am thirsty.”
A container full of vinegar was standing there. They put a sponge soaked in vinegar on a hyssop stalk and held it up to his mouth.
When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, “It is completed.” He bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

Because it was the day of Preparation, the Jews asked Pilate to have their legs broken and their bodies taken away, so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath. For that Sabbath was a great day.
The soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man and of the other man who had been crucified with him.
But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.
The one who saw it has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he is telling the truth, so that you too may believe.
For these things happened so that the scripture would be fulfilled: “Not a single bone in him will be broken.”
And again the scripture says, “They will look at the one they pierced.”

After these things, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly because he feared the Jews, asked Pilate for permission to take away Jesus’ body. Pilate gave him permission. Then they came and took away his body.
Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus at night, also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes weighing about a hundred pounds.
They took Jesus’ body and wrapped it in cloths with the spices, according to the Jewish custom of preparing bodies for burial.
There was a garden at the place where he had been crucified, and in the garden there was a new tomb in which no one had yet been placed.
Because it was the Jewish day of Preparation, and because the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus in it.
On Sunday, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early in the morning, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance to the tomb.
She ran and came to Simon Peter and the other disciple, whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and I do not know where they have put him.”
Peter and the other disciple went out and headed toward the tomb.
They were running together, but the other disciple ran faster than Peter and reached the tomb first.
He looked inside and saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.
Simon Peter also arrived, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the cloths lying there.
And the cloth that had been wrapped around his head was not lying with the other cloths, but was rolled up separately by itself.
Then the other disciple, who had arrived first, also went into the tomb. He saw and believed.
For they had not yet understood the scripture that he must rise from the dead.
The disciples went back home.
But Mary was standing outside the tomb, weeping. As she wept, she looked into the tomb.
She saw two angels in white clothes sitting where Jesus’ body had been, one at his head and one at his feet.
They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “Because they have taken my Lord, and I do not know where they have put him.”
When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?” Thinking that he was the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have put him, and I will take him.”
Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said in Hebrew, “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.”
Jesus said to her, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet gone up to my Father. But go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am going up to my Father, who is your Father, and my God, who is your God.’”
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples, “I have seen the Lord, and he said these things to me.”

On the evening of that Sunday, the doors of the place where his disciples had gathered were shut because they were afraid of the Jews. Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”
When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
He said to them again, “Peace be with you. Just as my Father sent me, I too am sending you.”
When he had said this, he breathed into their faces and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.”
“Those whose sins you forgive will have their sins forgiven. Those whose sins you retain will have their sins retained.”
But Thomas, one of the twelve, who was called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples were telling him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see the nail marks in his hands, put my finger on the nail marks, and put my hand on his side, I will not believe.”
Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came while the doors were shut, stood among them, and said to them, “Peace be with you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Bring your finger here and look at my hands. Bring your hand and put it on my side. Do not be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”
Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples that are not written in this book.
But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and so that, by believing, you may receive eternal life in his name.
After these things, Jesus revealed himself again to his disciples by the Sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself in this way:
Simon Peter, Thomas who was called Didymus, Nathanael from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We are coming with you too.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing.
When morning came, Jesus stood on the shore, but the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.
Jesus said to them, “Little children, do you have any fish?” They answered him, “No.”

He said to them, “Cast your net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” But they said, “We have worked hard all night and caught nothing. But at your word we will cast it.” So they cast it, and they were unable to pull it up because of the great number of fish.

Then the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he tied his outer garment around himself, for he was naked, and threw himself into the sea.
The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from shore, but about two hundred cubits away.
When they came ashore, they saw a charcoal fire with a fish on it, and bread lying there.
Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish you have just caught.”
Simon Peter went aboard and pulled the net ashore. It was full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three in all. Although there were so many fish, the net did not tear.
Jesus said to them, “Come and eat.” None of the disciples dared to ask him, “Who are you?” because they knew that it was the Lord.
Jesus came, took the bread, and gave it to them, and likewise some of the fish.
This was the third time Jesus revealed himself to his disciples after he rose from the dead.
When they had eaten, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him a third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was saddened because he had said to him a third time, “Do you love me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

“Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and go wherever you wanted. But when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and take you where you do not want to go.”
He said this to indicate the kind of death by which he would glorify God. After saying this, he said to him, “Follow me.”
Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following him—the one who had leaned against Jesus’ chest at supper and said to him, “Lord, who is going to betray you?”
When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, and this man—[?]”
Jesus said to him, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.”
So this saying spread among the brothers: that disciple would not die. But Jesus had not said to him that he would not die, but, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?”
This is the disciple who testifies about these things and who wrote them down, and we know that his testimony is true.

There are also many other things that Jesus did. If they were written down one by one, I say that the world could not hold the books that would be written.
The Gospel according to John.
